    Presets and comparison with observed graphs¶

    The presets are specifications built from published Slide-recon arrays. This tutorial draws a few realizations of one of them and compares them with the summary of the observed graph. Generating a full-size graph takes about half a minute on one core, so the whole notebook takes a couple of minutes.

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import bipgen

bipgen.presets.available()
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import bipgen bipgen.presets.available()
    Out[1]:
    ['c58_16', 'c58_4', 'c58_5', 'slidetags_tonsil']

    An ensemble¶

    Three realizations: enough to see the spread, not to estimate tails.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    ensemble = [bipgen.generate(spec, seed=s) for s in range(3)]
for g in ensemble:
    print(g, f"expected / target edges = {g.info['expected_edges'] / g.info['target_edges']:.3f}, "
             f"sampled in {g.info['timing']['total']:.0f} s")
    ensemble = [bipgen.generate(spec, seed=s) for s in range(3)] for g in ensemble: print(g, f"expected / target edges = {g.info['expected_edges'] / g.info['target_edges']:.3f}, " f"sampled in {g.info['timing']['total']:.0f} s")

    Comparison with the observed graph¶

    presets.observed holds the statistics and degree sequences of the observed graph, so the comparison does not need the raw data. The z-score places the observed value in the ensemble.

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    observed = bipgen.presets.observed("c58_4")
table = bipgen.compare(observed, ensemble)
table.round(3)
    observed = bipgen.presets.observed("c58_4") table = bipgen.compare(observed, ensemble) table.round(3)

    Copied! 
    bipgen.plot_comparison(table);
    bipgen.plot_comparison(table);

    The realizations have about 0.4% fewer edges than the observed graph: this is the loss from clipping probabilities at 1 (expected_edges above). Realizations differ from each other so little that this small gap is many standard deviations. Clipping also caps the largest degrees, which stay below the observed maxima. Statistics with no spread in the ensemble, such as the numbers of nodes, have no z-score.

    Degree distributions: the distance from the observed degrees, next to the distance between two realizations, which is what sampling alone produces.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    bipgen.degree_ks(observed, ensemble).round(4)
    bipgen.degree_ks(observed, ensemble).round(4)

    A specification from your own graph¶

    spec_from_graph takes a biadjacency matrix (BCN as rows, TGT as columns) and reads off sizes and degree sequences; the kernel scale and the background are chosen by hand. Here a generated graph stands in for an observed one. With known positions of some nodes (positions=), the density is measured as well and positions are drawn with the Metropolis method.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    observed_graph = bipgen.generate(bipgen.spec_from_dict({
    "sizes": {"n_bcn": 1500, "n_tgt": 2000},
    "degrees": {"distribution": "lognormal", "bcn": {"median": 12, "sigma": 0.6},
                "tgt": {"sigma": 0.6}},  # shape only: scale set by the BCN total
    "edges": {"model": "kernel", "scale": 0.15},
}), seed=3)
fitted = bipgen.spec_from_graph(observed_graph.biadjacency, scale=0.15)
replicas = [bipgen.generate(fitted, seed=s) for s in range(10)]
bipgen.compare(observed_graph.biadjacency, replicas).round(3)
    observed_graph = bipgen.generate(bipgen.spec_from_dict({ "sizes": {"n_bcn": 1500, "n_tgt": 2000}, "degrees": {"distribution": "lognormal", "bcn": {"median": 12, "sigma": 0.6}, "tgt": {"sigma": 0.6}}, # shape only: scale set by the BCN total "edges": {"model": "kernel", "scale": 0.15}, }), seed=3) fitted = bipgen.spec_from_graph(observed_graph.biadjacency, scale=0.15) replicas = [bipgen.generate(fitted, seed=s) for s in range(10)] bipgen.compare(observed_graph.biadjacency, replicas).round(3)
